## What is a Matrix?

A **matrix** is an **array** with $R$ rows and $C$ columns. A matrix is typically denoted with an **upper case bolded** letter. For example

$$\mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 & 6 \\ 12 & -4 & 2 \\ 7 & -15 & 72 \\ -4 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Is a $4 \times 3$ matrix.

## Vectors and Scalars

A vector is an $R \times 1$ matrix. You might think of a vector as being like a single column. A vector is typically denoted with a lower case **bolded** letter. For example

$$\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 12 \\ 7 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix}$$

A single number is referred to as a **scalar**. It is typically denoted with an **un**bolded lower case letter. For example

$$x = 5$$


## Matrix Addition

Matrices of the same size can be added element-wise

Example: 

$$\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4\\
2 & 5\\
3 & 6
\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}7 & 10\\
8 & 11\\
9 & 12
\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1+7 & 4+10\\
2+8 & 5+11\\
3+9 & 6+12
\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8 & 14\\
10 & 16\\
12 & 18
\end{bmatrix}$$

- Results in a matrix of the same size

- Addition is not defined if matrices are not the same size


## Matrix Multiplication

Matrix multiplication is more complicated than matrix addition. 

- DO NOT multiply element-wise

- Order matters (commutative property does not hold) ($\mathbf{AB} \neq \mathbf{BA}$)
  
- The number of <u>columns</u> in the first matrix must equal the number of <u>rows</u> in the second matrix
  
- Results in a matrix with the same number of <u>rows</u> as the first matrix and the same number of <u>columns</u> as the second matrix

::: columns

:::: column

If $\mathbf{A}_{2\times 3}$ and $\mathbf{B}_{3 \times 5}$:

- $\mathbf{AB}$ has 2 rows, 5 columns

- $\mathbf{BA}$ is not defined

::::

:::: column

If $\mathbf{A}_{2\times 3}$ and $\mathbf{B}_{3 \times 2}$:

- $\mathbf{AB}$ has 2 rows, 2 columns

- $\mathbf{BA}$ has 3 rows, 3 columns

::::

:::

## Matrix Multiplication

Example: $\mathbf{A}_{2\times 3}$, $\mathbf{B}_{3\times 2}$

$$\mathbf{AB} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & 5\\ 2 & 4 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 10\\8 & 11\\9 & 12\end{bmatrix} = \\ \begin{bmatrix}1\times7+3\times8+5\times9 & 1\times10+3\times11+5\times12\\
2\times7+4\times8+6\times9 & 2\times10+4\times11+6\times12
\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}76 & 103\\
100 & 136
\end{bmatrix}$$

## Matrix Multiplication

Example: $\mathbf{A}_{2\times 3}$, $\mathbf{B}_{3\times 2}$

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

$$\mathbf{BA} = \begin{bmatrix}7 & 10\\8 & 11\\9 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & 5\\2 & 4 & 6\end{bmatrix} = \\ \begin{bmatrix}7\times1+10\times2 & 7\times3+10\times4 & 7\times5+10\times6\\
8\times1+11\times2 & 8\times3+11\times4 & 8\times5+11\times6\\
9\times1+12\times2 & 9\times3+12\times4 & 9\times5+12\times6
\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}27 & 61 & 95\\
30 & 68 & 106\\
33 & 75 & 117
\end{bmatrix}$$

:::

```{r}
#| eval: false

A <- matrix(1:6, 2, 3)
B <- matrix(7:12, 3, 2)
A %*% B
B %*% A
```

## Matrix Transpose

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

Matrix transpose: 

- Rows become columns, columns become rows

- Denoted with the "$T$" superscript: $\mathbf{A}^T$ is the transpose of $\mathbf{A}$

$$\mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4\\
2 & 5\\
3 & 6
\end{bmatrix} \qquad \mathbf{A}^T=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3\\
4 & 5 & 6
\end{bmatrix}$$

Multiplying a matrix by its transpose is a generalization of **squaring**

A **symmetric** matrix is a square matrix for which $\mathbf{A}^T = \mathbf{A}$. Example:

$$\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\
1 & 4 & 5 & 6\\
2 & 5 & 7 & 8\\
3 & 6 & 8 & 9
\end{bmatrix}$$

::: 

## Matrix Inverse

$\mathbf{I}$ is an **identity matrix** (generalization of the number '1'), a square matrix with 1's on the main diagonal and 0's on the off-diagonals. Example:

$$\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}$$

Matrix inverse:

- Defined only for square matrices

- $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ is the matrix inverse of $\mathbf{A}$

- $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{I}$

## Inverse Example

$$\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\\
2 & 5
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -2\\
-2 & 1
\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}$$
